channel.title: Anatomy Nexus health blog
channel.description: Guides to common conditions, medicines and tests, and plain-English summaries of the latest health announcements, each with its sources.

item.title: eGFR and creatinine: kidney test results
item.description: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.

item.title: X-ray: what to expect, safety and results
item.description: An X-ray uses a small beam of radiation to picture bones, lungs and other parts. This guide covers the test, radiation risk, pregnancy and results.

item.title: Why antibiotics do not work for colds, flu and most coughs, and what the NHS says instead
item.description: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so the NHS says they do not help colds, flu or most coughs and sore throats.

item.title: Travel vaccinations: what the NHS says about which are needed and when to arrange them
item.description: The NHS advises getting travel vaccine advice several weeks before departure, as needs depend on the destination, and some vaccines are free while others are paid for.

item.title: Choosing between 999, NHS 111, a GP, a pharmacy and urgent care
item.description: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies and NHS 111 for urgent problems or when unsure, with pharmacies, GPs and urgent treatment centres for others.

item.title: Jet lag: what it is, why it happens and what the NHS says helps
item.description: Jet lag is a temporary sleep disturbance after long flights across time zones; the NHS says it usually improves within a few days.

item.title: Taking warfarin or apixaban: why other medicines and food matter
item.description: Bleeding is the main risk of both, so the NHS says other medicines, alcohol and, for warfarin, some foods and INR blood tests all matter.

item.title: Vitamins and supplements: who the NHS says may need them
item.description: The NHS says a varied and balanced diet should provide enough of several vitamins, but advises supplements for some people, including vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid in early pregnancy.

item.title: Vitamin D blood test: who needs one?
item.description: NHS guidance does not recommend routine vitamin D tests for people without symptoms, and testing is kept for specific symptoms or conditions.

item.title: Vitamin B12 and folate tests explained
item.description: Blood tests for B12 and folate help diagnose deficiency, but a B12 test can miss cases, so symptoms matter too.

item.title: Losing weight without trying: possible causes and when to see a GP
item.description: Losing weight without changing diet or exercise has many causes, from stress to thyroid or digestive conditions. The NHS advises seeing a GP as a precaution.

item.title: Underactive and overactive thyroid compared: symptoms, causes and treatment
item.description: An underactive thyroid does not make enough thyroid hormone, while an overactive thyroid makes too much; the symptoms, causes and treatments differ.

item.title: Ultrasound scan: what happens and is it safe
item.description: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves, not radiation, to make live pictures. This guide covers the gel, the full bladder, internal scans and results.

item.title: Urinary tract infection and cystitis: symptoms, treatment and when to get help
item.description: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys; cystitis is a UTI of the bladder, and antibiotics are not always needed.

item.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared: causes, symptoms and treatment
item.description: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition treated with insulin; type 2 develops when the body makes too little insulin or it works poorly.

item.title: Troponin blood test: what it shows
item.description: A troponin test measures proteins released when heart muscle is damaged, and a raised result does not always mean a heart attack.

item.title: Planning, packing and paperwork for medicines when travelling, as the NHS and TravelHealthPro describe
item.description: The NHS and TravelHealthPro describe original packaging, hand luggage, a prescriber's letter and checking the rules of each destination country.

item.title: Tiredness that will not go away: common causes and what a GP checks
item.description: Tiredness is common and often has an ordinary cause such as poor sleep, stress or illness. The NHS advises a GP appointment when it lasts a few weeks without explanation.

item.title: Thyroid blood tests: TSH and T4 explained
item.description: Thyroid tests read TSH and free T4 together, because free T4 helps to interpret an abnormal TSH.

item.title: The Eatwell Guide: what a balanced diet looks like in the UK
item.description: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups in a balanced UK diet, with fruit, vegetables and starchy foods making up just over a third each.

item.title: Testicle lumps and swelling: what to check
item.description: The NHS says to check your testicles monthly for changes; a lump or swelling needs a GP visit, and sudden severe pain needs A&E or 999.

item.title: Teething in babies: signs and what helps
item.description: The NHS lists sore red gums, a flushed cheek and extra dribbling as signs of teething, and suggests gum massage or a cool teething ring.

item.title: Swollen ankles, feet and legs: common causes and when to get help
item.description: Swollen ankles and legs often come from sitting or standing for long periods, but can signal a clot or a heart, kidney or liver problem. The NHS names the signs that need 111 or 999.

item.title: Supporting someone with a mental health problem
item.description: Listening, asking open questions and offering practical help are the NHS's main suggestions for supporting someone with a mental health problem, without forcing them to talk.

item.title: Sun safety and checking your skin: what the NHS and Cancer Research UK say
item.description: The NHS advises sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and 4-star UVA protection alongside shade and clothing, and describes changing moles as a reason to see a GP.

item.title: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs and why 999 is the route
item.description: A stroke and a TIA are both emergencies: the NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 even if the symptoms pass.

item.title: Stress: how it affects the body and mind, and where to get help
item.description: Stress is a reaction to mental or emotional pressure that can affect mood, body and behaviour, and the NHS says support is available when it affects daily life.

item.title: Stopping smoking: what support the NHS offers and what to expect
item.description: NHS stop smoking services offer nicotine replacement, medicines and professional support, and people in England can self-refer through NHS Better Health.

item.title: Stomach ache: causes by area and warning signs
item.description: Where a stomach ache sits helps point to causes such as appendicitis, gallstones or IBS, and sudden severe pain needs 999 or A&E.

item.title: Statins: what they do and the common concerns, as the NHS describes them
item.description: The NHS says statins lower the cholesterol the body makes, to reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, and they are usually taken long term.

item.title: Sprains and strains: how they are treated and when it is more than a sprain
item.description: The NHS describes PRICE care for the first 2 to 3 days, and most sprains and strains feel better after about 2 weeks.

item.title: Spirometry: the lung function test explained
item.description: Spirometry measures how much air can be blown out and how fast. This guide covers the test, preparation and what results are compared with.

item.title: Sore throat: causes, treatment, when to act
item.description: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and clear up on their own, but struggling to breathe or swallow needs 999 or A&E.

item.title: Sleep problems: what helps and when to get help
item.description: The NHS says insomnia usually improves by changing sleeping habits, and that a GP can arrange CBT when habits alone do not help.

item.title: Shortness of breath: causes and next steps
item.description: Breathlessness has many causes, from asthma and infections to heart and lung disease, and severe difficulty breathing needs a 999 call.

item.title: Sepsis: the warning signs in adults and children and when to call 999
item.description: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection; the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis is suspected.

item.title: Sedating and non-sedating antihistamines
item.description: The NHS lists chlorphenamine as sleep-inducing and cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine as non-drowsy, though cetirizine can still cause sleepiness.

item.title: Reliever and preventer inhalers: what is the difference?
item.description: A reliever inhaler eases symptoms when they happen, while a preventer is taken every day to reduce airway inflammation.

item.title: Puberty: what happens and when to get advice
item.description: Puberty brings body and mood changes at different ages, and NHS pages advise a GP appointment if it starts early or seems late.

item.title: Protecting your hearing from loud noise: headphones, earplugs and warning signs
item.description: The WHO and NHS sources say noise-related hearing loss is permanent but can be prevented, mainly by lowering volume, taking breaks and using ear protection.

item.title: Prostate problems: symptoms and seeing a GP
item.description: Prostate symptoms are mostly urinary, such as a weak flow or going more often. Causes include enlargement, infection and cancer.

item.title: Preventing food poisoning at home: cleaning, cooking, chilling and cross-contamination
item.description: NHS inform and the Food Standards Agency describe four steps for food safety at home: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination.

item.title: Preparing for a blood test: fasting explained
item.description: Some blood tests need fasting or a change to what you eat, drink or take beforehand; the person who arranges the test should say which applies.

item.title: Pregnancy scans and tests on the NHS
item.description: NHS pregnancy care includes booking blood tests, a dating scan and a mid-pregnancy anomaly scan, plus optional screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes.

item.title: Periods: what is normal and when to see a GP
item.description: The NHS gives an average cycle of about 28 days. A GP can help if periods change, become painful or stop.

item.title: Pelvic pain in women: common causes, red flags and which NHS route to use
item.description: Pelvic pain in women often comes from period pain, ovarian cysts or endometriosis, but a few causes are serious. The NHS says to call 999 for severe or worsening pain.

item.title: Panic attacks: what they are and what helps
item.description: A panic attack is a rush of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat. The NHS describes how attacks pass and how talking therapy and medicine can treat repeated attacks.

item.title: PSA test: what it shows and what the NHS says
item.description: A PSA test measures prostate-specific antigen in the blood. The NHS says it is not a routine screening test, and results can be wrong in both directions.

item.title: PET and bone scans: what to expect
item.description: PET and bone scans both use a small amount of radioactive tracer given by injection. Both scans involve a waiting period after the injection.

item.title: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis: how they differ
item.description: Osteoarthritis makes joints painful and stiff; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the joint lining.
